biggestWin: Give the reading surface back to the document scroller. Right now the whole page lives inside .scroll (height:100vh; overflow-y:auto) while html/body are pinned to 100% height, so on a fresh load — nothing clicked, focus on body — Space, PageDown, ArrowDown and End all scroll exactly zero at every width and in every state. 664px of the full state is unreachable that way at 1440 and 1,820px at 390. It is one structural change (sticky rail, body scrolls) and it is the only defect I found that touches every state, every width and every reader rather than one region. Second on the list, and the one a founder will actually feel: the KPI row is the surface's only interactive region and every state it declares — hover lift, press — is dead on arrival, so the row currently behaves like decoration that happens to take focus.

findings.element: The scroll container — .scroll (lately.html:171), inside .canvas (:170) and .app (:153), with html, body { height: 100% } (:116)
findings.problem: The document itself has zero scrollable overflow: html and body are locked to 100% height and every pixel of the page sits inside .scroll, a div with height:100vh and overflow-y:auto that is not focusable and carries no tabindex. Chrome routes an un-targeted key scroll to the document's scrolling element, which cannot move. Driven in chromium on a fresh load with nothing clicked and document.activeElement === BODY, Space, PageDown, ArrowDown and End each left .scroll.scrollTop at 0 — measured on full@1440 (664px of overflow), full@390 (1,820px), loading@390 (1,021px) and partial@1440 (759px). The wheel works (400px), and so does the keyboard, but only after the reader has clicked inside the region or pressed Tab far enough to put focus inside it: after one Tab onto the tab strip, PageDown moved 664px at 1440 and 736px at 390.
findings.consequence: A reader who opens Lately and presses the gesture every reading surface answers to — space bar, page down — gets nothing, at any width, in any state. On the phone that hides 1,820 of 2,664px: the KPI row, the ages strip and the whole 'What this can't tell you' movement are below a fold the primary gesture will not cross. A keyboard-only reader recovers only by discovering that Tab first, then PageDown, works, which nothing on screen tells them. This is a reading instrument whose reading gesture is dead until you interact with it some other way.
findings.fix: Make the document the scroller and let the rail stay put. In the stylesheet: change `html, body { height: 100%; }` (:116) to `html { height: 100%; } body { min-height: 100%; }`; change `.app` (:153) to `min-height: 100vh`; add `position: sticky; top: 0; height: 100vh; align-self: flex-start;` to `.rail` (:155); drop `overflow: hidden` from `.canvas` (:170); and reduce `.scroll` (:171) to `overflow-x: clip;` — deleting `height: 100vh` and `overflow-y: auto`. Nothing in the script needs changing: the tooltip's scroll listener is already bound to window with capture:true, so it receives the document's scroll event exactly as it received the container's, and .reading / .strip are measured from getBoundingClientRect either way.
findings.assertion: For every state in config.states and every declared viewport: open the master fresh, assert nothing has been clicked and document.activeElement is document.body, record the scroll offset, press PageDown, and assert the offset increased by at least 80% of the viewport height whenever document.documentElement.scrollHeight - clientHeight > 0. Repeat for Space and for End (End must reach the bottom). Watch it fail against the current file first.

findings.problem: `.rise` sets `animation: rise 0.5s var(--ease) both`, and rise's `to` frame is `{ opacity: 1; transform: none }`. A filled animation sits in the animation origin, which outranks any plain author declaration, so `transform` on every .rise element is pinned to `none` forever. The KPI cards carry `.rise`, so `a.kpi:hover { transform: translateY(-2px) }` has never painted. Driven with real pointer travel and a held mouse-down in all three motion modes — settled (automation default), ?motion=play, and prefers-reduced-motion — the computed transform on a.kpi read matrix(1,0,0,1,0,0) at rest, on hover and on press, identically. The press is dead twice over: `a.kpi:active { transform: translateY(0) }` is the rest value anyway, so even released it would change nothing. The whole hover channel that survives is a 1px border stepping rgba(17,17,17,0.055) → 0.10 (#f2f2f2 → #e8e8e8 on white); on press, computed transform, background-color and border-color are byte-identical to hover. This is the same mechanism the file's own comments record twice (':290 — a clip-path keyframe with fill:both outranks any plain author declaration'; the r1 fix of record-tag-never-paints) and it has come back on the one interactive region on the screen. The gate does not see it: interaction-check.mjs:1313-1325 proves the press by string-matching 'a.kpi:active' in document.styleSheets, so 'every control acknowledges a press' passes on a rule that has never painted — L-06, a gate that has never failed.
findings.consequence: Hovering the card that names the reader's biggest problem — '3 haven't moved in a fortnight' — produces a hairline going from 4% to 7% ink and nothing else, so the card reads as a static tile rather than something you can act on. Pressing it produces no acknowledgement at all. On a phone, where the gate's own comment says a press is the only channel that can confirm a touch landed, tapping the card gives the reader nothing: the tap leaves the card in its hover border and no press moment ever happens. Every state this row declares is decoration in the source and absent on screen.
findings.fix: Release the class when its entrance ends, so transform returns to the author cascade. In the render block, after the skeleton fix-ups (lately.html:1151), add: `for (const el of root.querySelectorAll('.rise')) el.addEventListener('animationend', (e) => { if (e.animationName === 'rise') el.classList.remove('rise'); }, { once: true });`. rise's end state is identical to the natural state (opacity 1, transform none), so nothing jumps; and it fires in settled and reduced-motion too, where the duration is 1ms. Then give the press a channel that does not depend on hover: replace `a.kpi:active { transform: translateY(0); }` (:325) with `a.kpi:active { transform: translateY(0); background: var(--paper-3); border-color: var(--ink-4); }` — both already in the lock and both already used by .btn:hover.
findings.assertion: After settle, assert every element that carried .rise has computed animation-name 'none'. Then, in each of the three motion modes (default, ?motion=play, reducedMotion), move a real mouse onto a.kpi and assert its computed transform differs from its rest transform; hold pointerdown and assert at least one of transform, background-color or border-color differs from the hover state. Break the fix and watch each of the four fail first.

findings.element: The status cards in 'What's quietly slipping' — the `known && n > 0` anchor branch in kpi() (lately.html:692-694)
findings.problem: A status card with a non-zero count renders as `<a class="kpi" href="#">`: link role, pointer cursor, focus ring, its own hover and active rules. A zero card renders as a `<div>`. At rest the two are pixel-identical — same paper, same hairline, same 34px numeral, same meter. Driven at 1440: clicking any of the three links, or pressing Enter on one, only appends '#' to the URL; the scroll position, the rendered surface and aria-current are all unchanged. So three of the four status cards look and read exactly like the fourth, take focus and a link role, and go nowhere — while the fourth, which is inert only because its count happens to be 0, gives no sign of it until you press it. In the first-run state the ratio inverts: one of the four is a link and three are not, again with nothing at rest to tell them apart. The round-2 notes state the opposite policy explicitly for the hero — 'The hero no longer says a finished job is openable, because nothing on this surface opens one. That is on the port packet, not on the screen' — and interaction-check.mjs:1290-1299 enforces it, but only against the word 'openable' in the rendered text, so a promise made in role, cursor and focus ring passes untouched.
findings.consequence: The reader presses the card naming the thing they came here to fix and the screen does not move — no list, no navigation, no message, not even a press. Having learned the cards are pressable, they press the one that is inert and get the same nothing, with no way to know the two nothings have different causes. A row of five identical tiles where three carry a link role and two do not is an affordance the reader cannot read at rest and cannot trust once pressed.
findings.fix:
Apply the decision already taken for the hero. In kpi() (:692-694) drop the branch and always return `
${body}
`; delete `a.kpi:hover`, `a.kpi:focus-visible` and `a.kpi:active` (:323-325) with them. Record the filtered-list destination on the port packet beside the hero's, so the affordance ships when the destination does. The row then reads as five figures over one denominator, which is what it is, and every card in it behaves the same way whatever its count.
findings.assertion: For every state, assert document.querySelectorAll('.kpi a, a.kpi').length === 0 — no card in the row carries a link role. And, as the general rule behind it: for every state, collect every element with a link or button role inside main, activate each with a real click and with Enter, and assert that each one either changes the rendered surface or changes location beyond appending a bare '#'.

findings.problem: The loading skeleton renders movements one and two and stops. Movement three — 'What this can't tell you', a protected object — is not in it, and it renders in full, partial, quiet and first-run alike. Measured in chromium: at 1440 the loading main is 832px and the main that arrives is 1,276px, two sections becoming three, +444px; at 390 it is 1,423px becoming 2,222px, +799px — 36% of the final page that the loading frame never promised. The conservative reading does not hold, because the skeleton already commits to the full state's shape: movements one and two do not render in the empty or error states either, and the skeleton draws them anyway. And movement three needs no source at all — LIMITS (:828-832) and the ghost columns (:835) are constants, true before any of the three sources answers.
findings.consequence: A reader who lands during the read sees a page that ends at the ages card. Everything the skeleton teaches them about the shape and the length of this screen is wrong by a third on a phone, and the movement that disappears is the one the product most wants read — the refusals. When the data lands the page grows 799px underneath them; if they had scrolled to what looked like the end, the end moves. A skeleton that lies about the length of the page is the same defect class as one that invents a section, pointed the other way.
findings.fix:
Render the refusals for real during the read rather than as skeleton: change VIEW.loading (:973-975) to `shell('
' + movementOne() + movementTwo() + '
' + movementThree() + '

Loading this reading.

')`. Movement three holds no read value, so it does not need its ink taking out; it arrives complete, the loading frame is the height of the page that follows, and the reader gets the one movement that is already true while the rest is being read.
findings.assertion: At every declared viewport, open ?state=loading and ?state=full, and assert document.querySelectorAll('main section').length is equal in both and that the rendered height of main differs by no more than 8px. Watch it fail at 390 (1,423 vs 2,222) against the current file.

findings.problem: The handler re-runs the de-swarm and the reading-line measurement and repositions the tooltip, but it never puts the focused element back on screen. Driven at 1440x960: focus the fifth mark, tip up and correctly placed 8px above it, then resize to 1280x844 — the mark is now at top 948 in an 844px window, 104px below the fold; at 768 it is at 1,457; at 390 it is at 1,570, 726px below the fold. In each case document.activeElement is still that mark and the tooltip has correctly hidden itself (onMove sees the mark out of view), so the reader is left with no visible focus ring anywhere on the screen and no label. This is the class the defect library names outright — 'Focus that leaves the screen: keep the focused element scrolled into view through every move' — creeping back through the one repaint path the surface has.
findings.consequence: A keyboard or screen-magnifier reader loses their place on a rotation or a window resize. The ring is gone from the screen, the mark's title — which lives nowhere else on this surface — is gone with it, and the only way back is to press Tab and land somewhere else entirely. On a phone, rotating to landscape and back is a routine gesture, and it costs the reader the position they had worked to reach.
findings.fix: Restore the focused element in the same handler, after the relayout that moved it. Replace :1072 with: `window.addEventListener("resize", () => { const held = document.activeElement; relayout(); if (held && held !== document.body && root.contains(held)) { const b = held.getBoundingClientRect(); if (b.top < 0 || b.bottom > window.innerHeight) held.scrollIntoView({ block: "nearest" }); } queueMove(); });` — queueMove already runs on the next frame, so the tooltip is placed against the restored position rather than the stranded one.
findings.assertion: At 1440x960, focus a mark below the fold, then set the viewport to 1280x844, 768x1024 and 390x844 in turn; after each, assert document.activeElement is unchanged and its bounding box lies wholly inside the viewport. Repeat with a focused KPI card. Watch the 1280 step fail against the current file (top 948 in an 844px window).

findings.element: The .sr span inside kpi() (lately.html:691), on the anchor branch (:692-694)
findings.problem: The card's visible numeral and phrase and the .sr sentence are both descendants of the same element, so on the anchor branch they concatenate into one accessible name. Read out of the CDP accessibility tree at 1440, full state: 'link | 3 haven't moved in a fortnight 3 jobs haven't moved in a fortnight, of 9 jobs open'; likewise '2 past the day they were due 2 jobs past the day they were due, of 9 jobs open' and '1 has nobody's name on it 1 job has nobody's name on it, of 9 jobs open'. The .sr span is doing its job — it adds the shared denominator — but as a descendant of a name-from-content element it also repeats the fact it was written to qualify. interaction-check.mjs asserts only that an accessible name exists, so the doubling is invisible to the gate.
findings.consequence: A screen-reader reader hears each of the row's cards twice, once as a fragment and once as a sentence — an 86-character link name where a 46-character one says everything. Navigating the row by links, which is how a link-role element is usually reached, means listening to the same fact five times to hear four figures.
findings.fix: Move the sentence onto the element instead of inside it. In kpi() (:675-695) drop `${esc(name)}` from `body`, and put the sentence on the container as an attribute: emit `aria-label="${esc(name)}"` on the returned element (whether it stays an anchor or becomes a div per kpi-cards-are-links-that-open-nothing) and add `role="group"` to the div branch so the label is honoured on a generic container. Do the same in leadKpi() (:699-707). The name then reads once, as the sentence that was written for it.
findings.assertion: For every state, for every .kpi, compute the accessible name and assert that no substring of eight or more characters appears in it twice, and that the name equals the sentence the card was authored with. Watch it fail on the three anchors in the full state first.
